steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for our paper on object detection in remote sensing images with limited labels. We combine semi-supervised learning and active learning on a teacher-student network; motivate the labeling problem, review SSL and AL, point out what earlier combinations miss, and summarize our method and contributions.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- Object detection in remote sensing images needs costly labels
- Semi-supervised learning and teacher-student SSOD
- Active learning and query criteria
- Combining SSL and AL: existing methods and their gap
- Our method SSOD-AT
- Contributions

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
- Labeling problem
  - object detection in RSIs: identify objects + locations (cite)
  - deep learning promising, but needs large-scale accurately labeled data from human experts
  - unlike classification: object-level labels = bounding box coordinates + categories; more laborious, time-consuming
  - various orientations and scales complicate labeling (cite several)
  - images faster/easier to collect, but labeled images usually limited (cite)
- SSL
  - SSL and AL: two promising techniques for limited labeled images
  - SSL: exploit unlabeled data with limited labeled data; assumes consistent feature distributions
  - most SSOD methods: teacher-student network; secondary model (teacher) guides primary model (student)
  - teacher: weakly augmented labeled data -> high-quality pseudo-labels (cite); student optimized on pseudo-labels
- AL
  - focuses on labeled data: select most informative unlabeled samples for expert labeling (cite)
  - core: query criterion, i.e. uncertainty and diversity (cite)
  - MI-AOD (Yuan et al.): instance-level uncertainty, highlight informative instances, filter noisy ones
  - CALD: individual information + mutual information against unbalanced class distribution -> diversity
  - MOL: temporal consistency-based instance selection, reliable foreground objects, less background interference
- Combining SSL + AL
  - SSL relies on labeled data to exploit unlabeled; AL labels most informative samples -> natural to combine for limited labeled RSIs
  - many methods in natural images
  - Lv et al.: semi-supervised active salient object detection (SOD), salient encoder-decoder + adversarial discriminator
  - Mi et al.: "Active Teacher", data initialization through AL with teacher-student SSOD
  - gap: ignore redundancy in RoIs -> more images selected
- SSOD-AT
  - Semi-Supervised Object Detection with Active Teaching; teacher-student network
  - large scale variations, high density -> noisy RoIs
  - RoI Comparison Module (RoICM): compare teacher vs student RoIs
  - consistent -> pseudo-labels; divergent -> image uncertainty from teacher predictions
  - diversity via global class prototype to remove redundancy
  - uncertainty + diversity = query score for human labeling
- Contributions
  - novel method boosting SSOD with AL for RSIs; confident pseudo-labels + informative images
  - RoICM: alleviate noisy RoIs for SSL, better uncertainty estimate for AL
  - global class prototype for diversity; combination of the two sampling strategies

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Object detection in remote sensing images is an important task, it identifies the objects and their locations. Deep learning has shown promising results for object detection in remote sensing images in recent years. But deep learning approaches need large-scale datasets with accurately labeled data to be successful, and these are typically annotated by human experts. Object detection is different from image classification because it needs object-level labels, which include both the bounding box coordinates and the object categories. So the annotation is more laborious and takes more time. Also, remote sensing images often have objects with various orientations and scales, and this makes the labeling even more complicated. So even though collecting remote sensing images is getting faster and easier with the advances in remote sensing technology, there are usually only a limited number of labeled images for object detection.

Semi-supervised learning (SSL) and active learning (AL) are two promising machine learning techniques for the problem of limited labeled images. SSL usually tries to exploit the unlabeled data with a limited amount of labeled data, and it assumes that the feature distribution of the unlabeled data and of the labeled data is consistent. Most semi-supervised object detection (SSOD) methods are based on a teacher-student network. In this network a secondary model (the teacher) is introduced to guide the training of the primary model (the student). The teacher network uses weakly augmented labeled data and generates high-quality pseudo-labels for the student network. Then the student network is optimized using the pseudo-labels as supervised information.

AL is different from SSL because it generally focuses on the labeled data. These are mainly collected by selecting the most informative samples from the unlabeled data and having human experts label them. The core technique in AL methods is the query criterion, i.e. uncertainty and diversity. Yuan et al. propose MI-AOD, which is an instance-level uncertainty-based method. It highlights the informative instances and filters out the noisy ones in order to select the most informative images for training the detector. CALD gauges individual information for sample selection, but it also uses mutual information to alleviate unbalanced class distribution, and so it ensures the diversity of the selected samples. MOL introduces an instance selection strategy based on temporal consistency to discover reliable foreground objects, which reduces the risk of background interference.

- Combining SSL + AL
  - SSL relies on labeled data to exploit unlabeled; AL labels most informative samples -> natural to combine for limited labeled RSIs
  - many methods in natural images: Lv et al. semi-supervised active SOD (salient encoder-decoder + adversarial discriminator); Mi et al. "Active Teacher" (AL data initialization, teacher-student SSOD)
  - gap: ignore redundancy in RoIs -> more images selected
- SSOD-AT
  - teacher-student network; noisy RoIs from large scale variations and high density
  - RoICM compares teacher vs student RoIs: consistent -> pseudo-labels; divergent -> image uncertainty from teacher predictions
  - diversity via global class prototype; uncertainty + diversity = query score
- Contributions
  - novel SSOD + AL method for RSIs; RoICM; global class prototype for diversity

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Object detection in remote sensing images is an important task, it identifies the objects and their locations. Deep learning has shown promising results for object detection in remote sensing images in recent years. But deep learning approaches need large-scale datasets with accurately labeled data to be successful, and these are typically annotated by human experts. Object detection is different from image classification because it needs object-level labels, which include both the bounding box coordinates and the object categories. So the annotation is more laborious and takes more time. Also, remote sensing images often have objects with various orientations and scales, and this makes the labeling even more complicated. So even though collecting remote sensing images is getting faster and easier with the advances in remote sensing technology, there are usually only a limited number of labeled images for object detection.

Semi-supervised learning (SSL) and active learning (AL) are two promising machine learning techniques for the problem of limited labeled images. SSL usually tries to exploit the unlabeled data with a limited amount of labeled data, and it assumes that the feature distribution of the unlabeled data and of the labeled data is consistent. Most semi-supervised object detection (SSOD) methods are based on a teacher-student network. In this network a secondary model (the teacher) is introduced to guide the training of the primary model (the student). The teacher network uses weakly augmented labeled data and generates high-quality pseudo-labels for the student network. Then the student network is optimized using the pseudo-labels as supervised information.

AL is different from SSL because it generally focuses on the labeled data. These are mainly collected by selecting the most informative samples from the unlabeled data and having human experts label them. The core technique in AL methods is the query criterion, i.e. uncertainty and diversity. Yuan et al. propose MI-AOD, which is an instance-level uncertainty-based method. It highlights the informative instances and filters out the noisy ones in order to select the most informative images for training the detector. CALD gauges individual information for sample selection, but it also uses mutual information to alleviate unbalanced class distribution, and so it ensures the diversity of the selected samples. MOL introduces an instance selection strategy based on temporal consistency to discover reliable foreground objects, which reduces the risk of background interference.

SSL usually relies on the labeled data to exploit the unlabeled data for learning the task, while AL aims to label the most informative samples from the unlabeled data with a query criterion. So it is natural to combine AL and SSL to improve the object detection performance with limited labeled RSIs. Actually, many methods have already been developed for SSOD with AL in natural images. Lv et al. proposed a semi-supervised active salient object detection (SOD) method that used a salient encoder-decoder with an adversarial discriminator to select the most representative data. Mi et al. introduced a method called "Active Teacher", which does data initialization through AL using a teacher-student-based SSOD approach. But these methods usually ignore the redundancy in the RoIs, and as a result more images are selected to improve the SSOD performance.

In this paper we propose Semi-Supervised Object Detection with Active Teaching (SSOD-AT), a method for object detection in remote sensing images that uses a teacher-student network. Remote sensing images often have objects with large scale variations and high density, and this easily produces noisy RoIs. We introduce a RoI Comparison Module (RoICM) to mitigate the impact of these noisy RoIs. It compares the RoIs generated by the teacher network and by the student network. When the teacher and student networks give consistent predictions for the RoIs, the RoIs are assigned pseudo-labels for semi-supervised training. When the predictions are divergent, we use the RoIs to calculate the uncertainty of the image based on the predictions of the teacher network. We also design a diversity by introducing a global class prototype, to remove the redundancy from the queried images and make sure the current query image is diverse from the selected images. Finally, the uncertainty and the diversity are integrated as the query score, which is used to select the most valuable images for human labeling. The main contributions of this article are the following:

- A novel method is proposed for remote sensing images that boosts semi-supervised object detection with active learning, based on the teacher-student network. It can provide both confident pseudo-labels and informative images.

- A RoI comparison module (RoICM) is introduced, which compares the RoIs generated by the teacher and student networks. It can effectively alleviate the influence of noisy RoIs for semi-supervised learning, and it improves the ability of active learning to evaluate the uncertainty of images.

- The method also incorporates the global class prototype for the diversity of the selected images. Combining the two sampling strategies maximizes the effectiveness of the AL process.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Object detection in remote sensing images is a crucial task to identify the objects together with their locations [1]. In recent years, deep learning has shown promising results in object detection for remote sensing images. However, the success of deep learning approaches heavily relies on large-scale datasets with accurately labeled data, which are typically annotated by human experts. Unlike image classification, object detection requires object-level labels that include both bounding box coordinates and object categories, so the annotation process is more laborious and time-consuming. Additionally, remote sensing images often contain objects with various orientations and scales [2], [3], [4], [5], [6], which further complicates labeling. Hence, although remote sensing images are becoming faster and easier to collect with the advancements of remote sensing technology, the availability of labeled images for object detection is usually limited [7], [8], [9].

Semi-supervised learning (SSL) and active learning (AL) are two promising machine learning techniques to address the problem of limited labeled images. SSL usually attempts to exploit the unlabeled data with a limited amount of labeled data, assuming consistency between the feature distributions of unlabeled and labeled data. Most semi-supervised object detection (SSOD) methods are developed based on a teacher-student network, which introduces a secondary model (teacher) to guide the training of the primary model (student). The teacher network uses weakly augmented labeled data to generate high-quality pseudo-labels for the student network [10], and the student network is then optimized using the pseudo-labels as supervised information.

Different from SSL, AL generally focuses on the labeled data, which are mainly collected by selecting the most informative samples from the unlabeled data for human experts to label [11]. The query criterion is the core technique in AL methods, i.e. uncertainty and diversity [12], [13]. Yuan et al. [14] propose MI-AOD, an instance-level uncertainty-based method which highlights informative instances while filtering out noisy ones to select the most informative images for detector training. CALD [15] not only gauges individual information for sample selection but also leverages mutual information to alleviate unbalanced class distribution, thus ensuring the diversity of the selected samples. MOL [16] introduces a temporal consistency-based instance selection strategy for discovering reliable foreground objects, reducing the risk of background interference.

We note that SSL usually relies on the labeled data to exploit the unlabeled data for task learning, while AL aims to label the most informative samples from the unlabeled data with a query criterion. It is therefore natural to combine AL and SSL to improve object detection performance with limited labeled RSIs. In fact, many methods have been developed for SSOD with AL in natural images. Lv et al. [17] proposed a semi-supervised active salient object detection (SOD) method that utilized a salient encoder-decoder with an adversarial discriminator to select the most representative data. Mi et al. [18] introduced the method "Active Teacher", which involves data initialization through AL using a teacher-student-based SSOD approach. However, these methods usually ignore the redundancy in the RoIs, so that more images have to be selected to improve SSOD performance.

In this paper, we propose Semi-Supervised Object Detection with Active Teaching, termed SSOD-AT, for object detection in remote sensing images using a teacher-student network. Remote sensing images often contain objects with large scale variations and high density, which easily produces noisy RoIs. To mitigate the impact of these noisy RoIs, we introduce a RoI Comparison Module (RoICM) that compares the RoIs generated by the teacher network and the student network. When the RoIs exhibit consistent predictions between the teacher and student networks, they are assigned pseudo-labels for semi-supervised training. Conversely, RoIs with divergent predictions are used to calculate the uncertainty of the image based on the teacher network's predictions. To remove the redundancy from the queried images, a diversity is designed by introducing a global class prototype, ensuring that the current query image is diverse from the selected images. Finally, we integrate the uncertainty and diversity as the query score to select the most valuable images for human labeling. The main contributions of this article can be summarized as follows:

- A novel method to boost semi-supervised object detection with active learning is proposed for remote sensing images based on the teacher-student network. The method provides both confident pseudo-labels and informative images.

- A RoI comparison module (RoICM) is introduced that compares the RoIs generated by the teacher and student networks. It effectively alleviates the influence of noisy RoIs on semi-supervised learning and improves the ability of active learning to evaluate the uncertainty of images.

- The proposed method further incorporates the global class prototype for the diversity of selected images. The combination of the two sampling strategies maximizes the effectiveness of the AL process.
